tools.name: performance
tools.mechanism: Standard scikit-learn metrics (accuracy/F1/ROC-AUC for classification, R2/RMSE/MAE for regression) computed by comparing the model's own predict()/predict_proba() output against the true labels on the held-out test set. Not an ethics evaluator -- provides the utility axis every trade-off in the profile is measured against.
tools.formula:
accuracy = (TP + TN) / n
f1 (macro) = mean_c 2·precision_c·recall_c / (precision_c + recall_c)
roc_auc = P(score(x⁺) > score(x⁻))
regression: r2 = 1 − Σ(y−ŷ)² / Σ(y−ȳ)²,  rmse = √mean((y−ŷ)²)

tools.name: fairness
tools.mechanism: Groups the model's test-set predictions by a declared sensitive attribute and compares outcomes across groups using fairlearn.metrics.MetricFrame (or the equivalent numpy computation if fairlearn isn't installed): for classification, selection rate (demographic parity) and TPR/FPR gap (equalized odds); for regression, MAE/MSE gap between groups, since selection rate isn't defined for a continuous target. Inspects PREDICTIONS only: it never looks at the model's weights or training process, so it can flag *that* a gap exists between groups but not *why*.
tools.formula:
selection_rate(g) = P(ŷ=1 | A=g)
TPR(g) = P(ŷ=1 | y=1, A=g)    FPR(g) = P(ŷ=1 | y=0, A=g)
demographic_parity_diff = max_g selection_rate(g) − min_g selection_rate(g)
equalized_odds_diff = max( max_g TPR − min_g TPR , max_g FPR − min_g FPR )
min_group_selection_rate = min_g selection_rate(g)
regression: group_mae_gap = max_g MAE(g) − min_g MAE(g)

tools.name: explainability
tools.mechanism: Two independent, model-agnostic signals, both treating the model as a black-box predict()/predict_proba() function -- neither inspects real internal weights: (1) surrogate fidelity -- a depth-3 decision tree is trained to mimic the model's own predictions; how accurately that tiny, human-readable tree reproduces them is the fidelity score. (2) feature attribution -- when SHAP is installed, mean |SHAP value| per feature from a permutation-based explainer run over a random sample against a background sample; falls back to the surrogate tree's own feature_importances_ if SHAP errors or isn't installed.
tools.formula:
surrogate T = DecisionTree(max_depth=3) fit on (X_test, f(X_test))
surrogate_fidelity = mean_i 1[T(x_i) = f(x_i)]       (regression: max(0, R²(f(x), T(x))))
SHAP: φ_j(x) = Σ_{S ⊆ F∖{j}} |S|!(|F|−|S|−1)!/|F|! · [f(S ∪ {j}) − f(S)]
attribution_j = mean_i |φ_j(x_i)|     (permutation-sampled approximation)

tools.name: robustness
tools.mechanism: Adds Gaussian noise (sigma x per-feature standard deviation) to every numeric test feature, repeated several times, and measures the fraction of predictions that stay the same (classification) or the relative change in predicted value (regression). Inspects BEHAVIOR under input perturbation only -- it says nothing about *why* a model is or isn't stable, and never touches categorical/text features.
tools.formula:
x̃ = x + ε,  ε_j ~ N(0, (σ · std_j)²)   for every feature j
agreement_r = mean_i 1[f(x̃_i) = f(x_i)]          (repeat r = 1..R)
perturbation_stability = mean_r agreement_r
regression: agreement_r = max(0, 1 − mean|f(x̃)−f(x)| / mean|f(x)|)

tools.name: membership_inference
tools.mechanism: Black-box membership-inference attack (Yeom et al. 2018 confidence/loss-threshold style -- the same feature-based approach TensorFlow Privacy's own attack module implements, run directly via scikit-learn since tensorflow-privacy has no Python-3.12-compatible release). Extracts a per-sample 'how well does the model fit this point' feature for the model's own training rows (known members) and held-out test rows (known non-members) -- confidence in the true class + log-loss for classification when predict_proba is available (else the weaker label-only correctness indicator), or negative squared/absolute error for regression. Balances member and non-member counts by subsampling, then fits a LogisticRegression attack classifier and scores it via k-fold out-of-fold prediction (so the attack's own accuracy is never inflated by testing on rows it trained on). Reports attack AUC and attack advantage (2*(accuracy-0.5), clipped at 0) -- 0 means the attack is no better than guessing from the class balance alone (no detectable membership leakage from this feature); higher means the model's outputs let an attacker tell training rows apart from held-out rows.
tools.formula:
per row: conf(x, y) = f(x)[y],  loss(x, y) = −log conf(x, y)
members M = n train rows, non-members N = n test rows (balanced)
attack a = LogisticRegression on [conf, loss] → P(member)   (k-fold out-of-fold)
membership_inference_auc = AUC(a(M ∪ N), 1[x ∈ M])
membership_inference_advantage = max(0, 2·(accuracy(a) − 0.5))   (= TPR − FPR at 0.5)

tools.name: giskard
tools.mechanism: Runs Giskard's automated scanner over a random sample of test rows, treating the model as a black-box predict_proba function: PerformanceBiasDetector auto-discovers data slices via loss-guided slicing and flags ones whose performance metric is significantly worse than the global average (-> fairness); NumericalPerturbationDetector and EthicalBiasDetector perturb feature values (noise, rescaling, protected-attribute swaps) and flag high failure rates (-> safety). Issues are weighted by severity (major=3/medium=2/minor=1) and summed per principle bucket. Deliberately skips the data-leakage detector -- see this module's docstring.
tools.formula:
giskard.scan(model, sample, only=[performance, robustness]) → issues
weight(issue) = 3 (major) | 2 (medium) | 1 (minor)
giskard_issue_score(principle) = Σ weight(issue) over issues mapped to that principle

tools.name: art_robustness
tools.mechanism: Runs a real black-box adversarial evasion attack (HopSkipJump, Chen et al. 2019, via the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox) against the fitted model treated as a label-only oracle -- no gradients or model internals are used, matching how an external attacker would actually query a deployed model. Wraps the model in art.estimators.classification.SklearnClassifier, then for a small sample of correctly-classified test rows searches for the smallest L2 perturbation that flips the prediction, within a tight iteration/query budget kept low so a full model-zoo sweep finishes in reasonable time (see this module's docstring for measured per-model timings). Reports the fraction of attacked rows the search could NOT flip within budget (higher = more robust) and, among the ones it did flip, the median perturbation size needed (higher = the attacker needed a bigger, more detectable change -- also more robust). Complements the existing RobustnessEvaluator's random-noise stability check with a worst-case, adversarially-searched one.

tools.name: drift_detection
tools.install_hint: pip install alibi-detect   (needs Python 3.12 or earlier)
tools.mechanism: Manufactures a synthetic covariate shift by adding shift_scale x (per-feature training std) to every feature of the test set (simulating a deployment population that has systematically drifted from the training population), then runs Alibi Detect's TabularDrift (per-feature Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, Bonferroni-corrected across features, reference = training data) against both the shifted and the original (unshifted) test set. Scores the detector's own reliability on this dataset (did it correctly flag the shifted set as drifted AND correctly leave the unshifted set alone?) and separately measures how much the model's own held-out performance metric degrades once that shift is present.
tools.formula:
x_shift = x_test + s ⊙ shift_scale · std_train,   s_j ∈ {−1, +1}
per feature j: KS statistic D_j = sup_t |F_ref,j(t) − F_test,j(t)|  → p_j
is_drift = min_j p_j < p_val / d          (Bonferroni over d features)
drift_detection_score = (1[is_drift(shifted)] + 1[¬is_drift(original)]) / 2
performance_retention = clip(1 − (perf_orig − perf_shift)/|perf_orig|, 0, 1)

tools.name: aif360
tools.mechanism: Wraps the test labels and the model's test predictions as two aif360 BinaryLabelDatasets over a binarised sensitive attribute (privileged = the value with the highest training base rate, unprivileged = all others), then reads group metrics off aif360.metrics.ClassificationMetric: disparate impact, statistical parity, equal-opportunity and average-odds differences, plus the individual-fairness Theil index and its between-group component. Inspects PREDICTIONS against ground truth, like fairlearn, but adds the 80%-rule ratio and an individual-level inequality measure fairlearn doesn't compute.
tools.formula:
P = privileged group, U = unprivileged group
disparate_impact = P(ŷ=1 | U) / P(ŷ=1 | P)             (1 = parity; < 0.8 fails the 80% rule)
disparate_impact_gap = |1 − disparate_impact|
statistical_parity_diff = P(ŷ=1 | U) − P(ŷ=1 | P)
equal_opportunity_diff = TPR(U) − TPR(P)
average_odds_diff = ½[(FPR(U) − FPR(P)) + (TPR(U) − TPR(P))]
theil_index = (1/n) Σ_i (b_i/μ) ln(b_i/μ),   b_i = ŷ_i − y_i + 1,  μ = mean(b)

principles.name: Fairness & Non-discrimination
principles.plain: The model treats different groups of people equitably and does not encode bias.

principles.name: Transparency
principles.plain: How the model was built and how it decides can be inspected and documented.

principles.name: Explainability
principles.plain: A human can understand why the model made a particular prediction.

principles.name: Privacy & Data Protection
principles.plain: The model does not leak or over-expose the personal data it was trained on.

principles.name: Safety, Security & Robustness
principles.plain: The model behaves reliably under noisy, shifted, or adversarial inputs.

principles.name: Accountability
principles.plain: There is a clear, documented owner and audit trail for the model's decisions.

principles.name: Human Oversight & Determination
principles.plain: Humans stay in control and can review, override, or appeal decisions.

principles.name: Inclusiveness & Diversity
principles.plain: The system works for people of all backgrounds and abilities, and small groups are not ignored.

principles.name: Sustainability & Well-being
principles.plain: The system benefits society and the environment and avoids broad harm.

checklists.name: Deon data-science ethics checklist
checklists.scope: The whole project lifecycle, written for the data-science team itself.

items.text: If people are the subject of the data, did they give informed consent to this use, and can they withdraw it?
Have sources of collection bias (who is over- or under-represented, and why) been considered?
Is collection and exposure of personally identifiable information kept to what the task needs?
Is there a way for affected people to find out about and query the data collected on them?
Is sensitive data protected (access control, encryption) and is there a plan if it leaks?
Can an individual's data be removed on request?
Is there a schedule for deleting data once it is no longer needed?
Have perspectives that might be missing from the team been sought (e.g. domain experts, affected communities)?
Has the data been checked for quality issues and biases that could skew results?
Are results presented honestly, including uncertainty and limitations?
Is the analysis reproducible and auditable (code, data versions, decisions recorded)?
Has the model been checked for proxy variables that stand in for protected attributes?
Has performance been compared across relevant groups, and are the fairness metrics chosen deliberately?
Does the optimisation metric reflect the real-world costs of each kind of error?
Can the model's decisions be explained in terms the affected people would understand?
Are the model's known shortcomings and biases communicated to decision makers?
Is there monitoring for drift, degraded performance and emerging bias after launch?
Is there a process for people to contest a decision and get it corrected?
Can the model be rolled back or switched off quickly if it causes harm?
Have likely misuses or unintended uses been identified and mitigated?

checklists.name: EU Assessment List for Trustworthy AI (ALTAI)
checklists.source: European Commission High-Level Expert Group on AI, 2020
checklists.scope: Self-assessment against the EU's seven requirements for trustworthy AI.

items.text: Are users told they are interacting with, or being assessed by, an AI system?
Is the oversight model defined (human-in-the-loop, on-the-loop, or in-command) and are overseers trained?
Can a human safely override or stop the system?
Have attacks (data poisoning, evasion, model extraction) and their impact been assessed?
Is there a fallback plan if the system fails or behaves unexpectedly?
Is accuracy measured, monitored and communicated, including how often it may be wrong?
Has a data-protection impact assessment been done, and is data minimised?
Are data quality, integrity and access controls documented?
Are datasets and processes documented well enough to trace a decision back (traceability)?
Can the system's decisions be explained to the people affected?
Are the system's purpose, capabilities and limits communicated to users?
Is there a strategy to avoid creating or reinforcing unfair bias in data and algorithm design?
Is the system accessible and usable by people with diverse abilities and backgrounds?
Were affected stakeholders consulted during design?
Has the environmental impact (energy, compute) of training and running the system been considered?
Has the impact on work, skills and society at large been assessed?
Can the system be independently audited (logs, documentation, access for auditors)?
Is there a risk-management process, and a named owner for trade-offs and decisions?
Is there an accessible mechanism for redress when the system causes harm?

checklists.name: Datasheets for Datasets
checklists.source: Gebru et al., Communications of the ACM 2021 (arXiv:1803.09010)
checklists.scope: Documentation of the dataset the model is trained and evaluated on.

items.text: Is it documented why the dataset was created, by whom, and who funded it?
Is it documented what each instance represents, how many there are, and whether it is a sample of a larger set?
Does the dataset identify sub-populations (e.g. by age, sex), and is their distribution documented?
Does it contain data that could identify people or is otherwise sensitive, and is that documented?
Is the collection mechanism, time frame and sampling strategy documented?
Were the people involved notified and did they consent; was an ethical review done?
Is all cleaning, labelling and preprocessing documented, with the raw data kept?
Are tasks the dataset should NOT be used for documented?
Could the composition or collection lead to unfair treatment of individuals or groups if used naively?
Is the licence / terms of use stated?
Is there a named maintainer, an erratum process, and a policy for updates and deletion requests?

checklists.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
checklists.source: US National Institute of Standards and Technology, NIST AI 100-1 (2023)
checklists.scope: Organisational risk management across the four RMF functions.

items.text: Are legal and regulatory requirements for this AI system understood and documented?
Are roles, responsibilities and lines of authority for AI risk clearly assigned?
Is workforce diversity and domain expertise considered in AI risk decisions?
Are policies in place for third-party data, models and software?
Is the intended purpose, context of use and the people affected documented?
Are the system's limitations and the conditions it must not be used under documented?
Are potential benefits and costs, including to individuals and society, characterised?
Are appropriate metrics chosen for each identified risk, and are their limits known?
Is the system evaluated for fairness, robustness, privacy and explainability (ethikit's own report counts as evidence)?
Are risks tracked over time after deployment?
Are identified risks prioritised and either mitigated, transferred or accepted with a documented rationale?
Are there mechanisms to supersede, disengage or deactivate the system?
Is there an incident-response and communication plan for when things go wrong?
